author: Shajaka Shelton
title: St. Johns man returns home after months in ICE custody - NewsBreak
text:
By Shajaka Shelton No media credit provided. ,
3 hours ago LANSING, Mich. (WLNS) — Lue Yang, a St. Johns father of six and Hmong refugee, returned home Wednesday after spending months in the custody of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement.
Lue Yang (middle), pictured with his family and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (left). (Courtesy Tom Barrett) Yang, 47, was detained by ICE while at work on July 15, sparking a four-and-a-half-month-long battle for his family, the Hmong community, and state and local officials to see him released.
Officials say Yang was born stateless in a refugee camp and came to Michigan legally in 1979 when his family was forced to flee political persecution after his father aided CIA activities in Laos.
He would later go on to reside in St. Johns and begin a career in the automotive industry, serving as the president of the Hmong Family Association of Lansing and an advocate for his community.
Yang’s detention stemmed from a 1997 criminal conviction for second-degree home invasion, for which he served a 10-month sentence. This conviction was expunged in 2018, but ICE can still access and use these records for the purposes of deportation cases. Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer pardoned him in October.
Wednesday, he arrived in Grand Rapids, much to the joy of his family and those who advocated for his release, including state Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren), herself a Hmong refugee.
“This battle for justice and due process for him and his family has been hard-fought, and I am so happy to see him reunited with his loving family, community and home state in time for the holiday season,” Xiong said.
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-07) represents the St. Johns area in Congress and says he worked with federal officials in the hopes of seeing Yang released.
“I’m so thankful that Lue was reunited with his family,” Barrett said. “Lue is not and never has been an illegal immigrant, and he does not present a threat to our community, which motivated me to work tirelessly to see him released from custody.”
Xiong says Yang’s situation is not unique and that other Hmong refugees that came to the U.S. may be facing similar circumstances.
“While there are still many members of our community that have been detained by ICE recently, his release today brings hope to so many immigrant families who are still awaiting their loved ones’ return home,” she said.
